LEARNING NOTEBOOK / AGILE PLANNING

One simple app.
Four levels of work.

An educational breakdown of registration, login, and a dashboard—from the reason we build to the tasks that make it happen.

Explore the breakdown ↓

Illustration only · This page does not create accounts or handle passwords.

01 / THE MODEL I’M USING

Theme → Epic → User story → Task

WHY

Theme

A broad user or business outcome.

Let people access their own private space.
WHERE / CAPABILITY

Epic

A larger collection of related stories. In this example, I group epics by screen.

Registration · Login · Dashboard
USER VALUE

User story

A small user goal, framed as who, what, and why.

As a registered user, I want to sign in so I can reach my dashboard.
HOW

Task

A concrete implementation or verification step that supports a story.

Verify the password hash and create a session.
A NOTE ON AGILE

For this illustration, an epic represents an entire screen and stories represent meaningful user actions on that screen. This is a useful teaching choice, not a universal Agile rule. Teams may define epics around capabilities that span screens. Typing a single character or clicking a field usually belongs inside a story rather than becoming its own user story.

02 / FOLLOW ONE CONSISTENT EXAMPLE

From the big picture
to the next task.

THEME T1

Simple account access

Allow a visitor to create an account, sign in, and use a private dashboard.

T1 → E1

Epic: Registration screen

Create an account so a new visitor can enter the app.

US1.1 Open registration

As a new visitor, I want to open registration so I can start creating an account.

Acceptance criteria

From the login page, selecting “Create account” opens the registration screen.

Implementation tasks

  1. US1.1.T1 — Add a Create account link to login.
  2. US1.1.T2 — Create the registration route and page heading.
  3. US1.1.T3 — Check that the link opens the correct screen.
US1.2 Create an account

As a new visitor, I want to submit my name, email, and password so I can create an account.

Acceptance criteria

Valid details create one account and send me to login with confirmation. A duplicate email or invalid input shows a clear error without creating another account.

Implementation tasks

  1. US1.2.T1 — Build labeled name, email, and password fields.
  2. US1.2.T2 — Validate inputs on the server and hash passwords securely.
  3. US1.2.T3 — Create the account with a unique email constraint.
  4. US1.2.T4 — Check valid, invalid, and duplicate-email submissions.
US1.3 Return to login

As a registered visitor, I want to return to login so I can sign in instead of registering again.

Acceptance criteria

Selecting “Already have an account? Log in” opens the login screen.

Implementation tasks

  1. US1.3.T1 — Add the return-to-login link.
  2. US1.3.T2 — Check its destination and keyboard access.

T1 → E2

Epic: Login screen

Let an existing user securely enter their account.

US2.1 Open login

As a registered user, I want to open login so I can access my account.

Acceptance criteria

The app entry URL opens login for a signed-out visitor; a signed-in visitor goes to the dashboard.

Implementation tasks

  1. US2.1.T1 — Create the login route and labeled form.
  2. US2.1.T2 — Redirect an existing valid session to the dashboard.
  3. US2.1.T3 — Check signed-in and signed-out entry behavior.
US2.2 Sign in

As a registered user, I want to submit my email and password so I can reach my dashboard.

Acceptance criteria

Correct credentials create a session and open the dashboard. Incorrect credentials show a generic error and keep me on login.

Implementation tasks

  1. US2.2.T1 — Verify the password hash on the server.
  2. US2.2.T2 — Create a secure session after successful verification.
  3. US2.2.T3 — Display a generic invalid-credentials message.
  4. US2.2.T4 — Check successful and unsuccessful sign-in.
US2.3 Go to registration

As a visitor without an account, I want to choose Create account so I can register.

Acceptance criteria

Selecting Create account opens the registration screen described by US1.1.

Implementation tasks

  1. US2.3.T1 — Reuse the registration link from US1.1.
  2. US2.3.T2 — Confirm the shared navigation acceptance check.

T1 → E3

Epic: Dashboard screen

Give a signed-in user a simple private home screen.

US3.1 View my dashboard

As a signed-in user, I want to see my name and a welcome message so I know I am in my account.

Acceptance criteria

A valid session shows the current user’s name. A signed-out request redirects to login without exposing account data.

Implementation tasks

  1. US3.1.T1 — Protect the dashboard route with a session check.
  2. US3.1.T2 — Load only the current user’s display name.
  3. US3.1.T3 — Render the welcome heading and account panel.
  4. US3.1.T4 — Check access with and without a valid session.
US3.2 Return to my dashboard

As a signed-in user, I want to refresh the dashboard so I can continue without signing in again.

Acceptance criteria

Refreshing with a valid session keeps me on my dashboard; an expired session sends me to login.

Implementation tasks

  1. US3.2.T1 — Restore the session on page requests.
  2. US3.2.T2 — Handle expired sessions consistently.
  3. US3.2.T3 — Check valid-session refresh and expired-session refresh.
US3.3 Log out

As a signed-in user, I want to log out so my account is protected when I leave.

Acceptance criteria

Log out invalidates the session and returns me to login. Revisiting or refreshing a protected page does not reveal account data.

Implementation tasks

  1. US3.3.T1 — Add a visible Log out button.
  2. US3.3.T2 — Invalidate the session on the server and clear its cookie.
  3. US3.3.T3 — Redirect to login and prevent caching of private responses.
  4. US3.3.T4 — Check that protected routes stay inaccessible after logout.

US2.3 and US1.1 refer to the same cross-screen navigation. A real backlog should link or reuse this work, not estimate and implement it twice. Clicking a button is only a story here when it expresses a meaningful navigation goal.

03 / HOW THE LEVELS CONNECT

Trace one action
all the way through.

Theme T1: Simple account access

↓ Epic E2: Login screen

↓ Story US2.2: As a registered user, I want to submit my email and password so I can reach my dashboard.

↓ Task US2.2.T1: Verify the password hash on the server.

Acceptance check: Correct credentials open the dashboard; incorrect credentials keep me on login with a generic error.

04 / HOW A TEAM WOULD USE THIS

Deliver a small working flow.
Then learn and refine.

Plan around a usable outcome

Refine and prioritize the stories, discuss dependencies, then select a realistic slice for the iteration. The smallest useful end-to-end flow connects registration, sign-in, dashboard access, and logout.

Screen-based epics help organize this example; they do not require building every screen separately before users can try the flow.

Check what “done” means

A story is done when its acceptance criteria are met and the team’s shared quality checks pass: reviewed code, appropriate tests, keyboard-friendly forms, server-side validation, and secure account/session handling.

Review the result with a user, collect feedback, and update the backlog. Tasks explain the implementation; acceptance criteria explain observable success.

05 / SCOPE BOUNDARY

Basic by design.

This example includes account creation, email/password sign-in, a welcome dashboard, and logout. Password reset, email verification, social login, roles, billing, and dashboard analytics would be separate future stories or epics.
